question: Only partly shared. Both papers compare MCI with healthy controls (and AD) on picture-description discourse. The record's contrast, however, sets P-747's co-speech hand-gesture rates, coded from video, against P-748's grammatical variables, coded from transcripts. Gesture is a motor behaviour, not the speech or language channel, so for that contrast the channels differ. The two papers share the speech/language channel only on generic lexical and fluency measures, and there the one variable both report is type/token ratio. The populations also differ: P-747 uses a Spanish clinic sample with MCI split into ex-MCI and tm-MCI; P-748 pools English SGUL, OPTIMA and DementiaBank Pitt samples with a single MCI group.
metric: Direction and significance of group differences in both (Kruskal-Wallis in P-747; ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis with Bonferroni-corrected pairwise tests and Cohen's d in P-748), but on different variables except type/token ratio.

figures.P-747: No gestural variable differs across the five groups (iconic gestures per minute p = 0.088, per word p = 0.060, iconic word substitution p = 0.088). Type/token ratio 0.39 (0.06) HC, 0.36 (0.08) ex-MCI, 0.38 (0.08) tm-MCI, p = 0.843. Group sizes are about 10-11, and no effect sizes or intervals are printed for the gesture variables.
figures.P-748: Adjunct clause ratio lower in MCI than HC (p = .003, d = .93); adverbial adjuncts lower in MCI (p = .020, d = .70). Type/token ratio does not differ (ANOVA p = .252; MCI vs HC pairwise p = 1, d = .08). Global measures (utterances, MLU, TTR, formal errors) do not distinguish the groups. 35 per group.

matched_figure_check: One matched figure exists, type/token ratio, and it reconciles the pair: both papers report no MCI-HC difference (P-747 p = 0.843; P-748 p = .252, MCI vs HC d = .08). No other variable is measured in both papers. P-748 records no gestures, and P-747 codes no grammatical structure.
performance_validity: Not a performance comparison: neither paper computes accuracy, AUC or any other discrimination statistic.
reason: The record's contrast, a null for co-speech gestures against positives for grammatical structure, compares different measured channels (video-coded hand gesture against transcribed grammar), so condition 1 fails for it. On the one language variable both papers measure, type/token ratio, both find no difference, so the matched figure reconciles them (condition 3). P-747 prints no effect sizes or intervals for its gesture nulls, so the remaining contrast is significance only (condition 4).

quotes.quote: the variables used were the counting of every type of gesture per minute of speech and the counting of every type of gesture per word.

Although no gestural variables did obtain sufficient statistical significance in terms of the five study groups distinction, it should be noted that three variables involving iconic gestures were found to have a tendency towards significance
Global measures of language (number of utterances, mean length of utterance (MLU), type-token ratio, and formal grammatical errors) did not distinguish groups.
